l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Chuang Tzŭ is described as treating Confucius with contempt and ridicule while also presenting Confucius as giving Taoist teachings. The unit proposes a remarkable parallel between Chuang Tzŭ's teaching and Heracleitus.

l: Mencius, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Mencius is presented as regarding Lao Tzŭ as a heresiarch, reflecting the growing divergence between Confucianism and Taoism.

l: Heracleitus, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Heracleitus is mentioned as a possible Western parallel to Chuang Tzŭ, because the writer sees a remarkable parallel between their teachings.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: TAO is described as 'the Way,' understood by Confucius through social duties and practical life and by Lao Tzŭ through the hidden and inward. The unit also states that 'the TAO which shines forth is not TAO.'

l: The Way, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: The Way is associated with TAO and is presented as something that cannot be fully identified with the way that is walked upon.

l: the triumph of Confucianism, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: The triumph of Confucianism is proposed as an explanation for the antagonism between Taoism and Confucianism. As Confucianism becomes established, Taoism is left out, suspected, or persecuted, and responds with scornful criticism and mystical protest.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The chapter presents transcendental bliss as freedom from dependence on self, action, reputation, and worldly distinctions. It contrasts the vast journeys of the Leviathan and Rukh with the limited understanding of smaller creatures, showing that magnitude and knowledge are relative. Emperor Yao, Hsü Yu, Chien Wu, Lien Shu, Hui Tzŭ, and Chuang Tzŭ illustrate different attitudes toward government, reputation, usefulness, and uselessness. The chapter concludes that things considered useless, such as a large gourd or an irregular tree, may possess greater freedom and value when viewed differently.

l: Transcendental Bliss, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Transcendental bliss is described as a state in which material existences, worldly joys, and sorrows cease to matter. It is associated with freedom from dependence on external things.

l: usefulness and uselessness, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The chapter teaches that usefulness depends on application and perspective. What appears useless may provide safety, freedom, or an unexpectedly valuable purpose.

l: Leviathan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The Leviathan is a fish in the northern ocean, several thousand li in size. It changes into the Rukh.

l: Rukh, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The Rukh is a gigantic bird whose back is many thousand li wide. It rises on a typhoon to ninety thousand li and flies for six months toward the southern ocean.

l: Celestial Lake, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The Celestial Lake is the southern ocean toward which the Rukh flies. It is also described as a great sea in the barren north.

l: T'ang, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Emperor T'ang tells Chi about the Leviathan and the Rukh to illustrate the difference between small and great.

l: Yung, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Yung is a philosopher who can distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic qualities and honour from shame. Even though he would not be changed by universal praise or blame, he has not established himself beyond the external world.

l: Lieh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Lieh Tzŭ can ride upon the wind and travel wherever he wishes, but he remains dependent upon the wind. He therefore has not attained complete freedom.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The perfect man ignores self. This teaching is presented as part of the path to transcendent peace.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The divine man ignores action and is described as inert, yet his influence fills creation, protects him from natural dangers, and causes crops to thrive.

l: Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The true Sage ignores reputation. Hsü Yu's refusal to take the throne illustrates this rejection of reputation.

l: Yao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Emperor Yao offers to abdicate in favour of Hsü Yu, believing that the empire will remain peaceful. After visiting the sages of the Miao-ku-shê mountain, he returns with the empire no longer existing for him as a worldly concern.

l: Hsü Yu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Hsü Yu refuses Emperor Yao's offer of the throne because reputation is only the shadow of reality. He compares taking over government to a corpse impersonator stepping over sacrificial food to do a cook's work.

l: Chien Wu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Chien Wu reports Chieh Yü's extravagant account of a divine man on Miao-ku-shê mountain. He regards the account as nonsensical and unbelievable.

l: Lien Shu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Lien Shu rebukes Chien Wu for judging the divine man with limited understanding. He explains that the divine man's influence is too great to be measured by ordinary worldly standards.

l: Miao-ku-shê mountain, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Miao-ku-shê mountain is said to be the home of a divine man whose body resembles ice or snow and who lives on air and dew. Emperor Yao visits its four sages and is transformed in his view of worldly possessions.

l: Hui Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Hui Tzŭ criticizes the large-sized gourd and a large tree of a worthless kind because they seem unusable. Chuang Tzŭ answers him with examples showing that unusual things may have value when properly applied.

l: large-sized gourd, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The large-sized gourd grows as large as a five-bushel measure. Hui Tzŭ breaks it up because it is too heavy for liquids and unsuitable as ladles, while Chuang Tzŭ says it could have been used as a boat.

l: salve for chapped hands, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: A family recipe for salve for chapped hands is sold by a silk-washing family to a stranger. The stranger uses it in war for the Prince of Wu, gaining territory and a title, showing that value depends on application.

l: large tree of a worthless kind, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The large tree has an irregular, knotty trunk and twisted branches, so carpenters consider it worthless. Chuang Tzŭ says it could be planted in the domain of non-existence, where its uselessness would protect it from harm.

l: domain of non-existence, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The domain of non-existence is presented as a place beyond the external world where one may practice inaction and rest beneath the shade of the useless tree.

l: reputation, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: Reputation is described as the shadow of reality and is rejected by Hsü Yu and the true Sage. The chapter treats freedom from concern with reputation as part of higher understanding.

l: self, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The perfect man ignores self. Emperor Yao's loss of concern for the empire illustrates a movement away from worldly self-interest.

l: action, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER I.
s: The divine man ignores action and remains inert while nevertheless influencing all creation and causing crops to thrive.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-kuo explains to Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu that the music of Heaven works through the natural distinctions and sounds of the universe. He argues that subjective and objective, affirmation and negation, and all contraries merge in TAO, whose axis lies where all distinctions become one. The true Sage follows Heaven by placing himself in subjective relation with external things, using the light of nature rather than fixed judgments. The unit also examines speech, mind, soul, Hui Tzŭ, and the rival claims of the Confucian and Mihist schools.

l: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-kuo, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-kuo buries himself in contemplation and explains the music of Man, Earth, and Heaven to Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu. He teaches that contraries and distinctions merge in TAO, and that the true Sage follows two courses at once.

l: Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu finds Tzŭ Ch'i leaning on a table as though his soul and body had parted. He questions Tzŭ Ch'i about the music of Heaven and receives his explanation.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: TAO is obscured by limited understanding and by speech shaped by worldly distinctions. Its axis is reached when subjective and objective lose their correlates, and all positive and negative distinctions blend into one.

l: Positive and Negative principles, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Contraries arise with individual bias and appear as affirmations and negations, subjective and objective, and other distinctions. The true Sage regards them as identical and reconciles them by the light of nature.

l: subjective, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The subjective is said to emanate from the objective and to be consequent upon it. Because each is also the other, their distinctions and correlates become indistinguishably blended.

l: objective, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The objective is said to emanate from the subjective and to be consequent upon it. It cannot be understood independently from subjective knowledge, since each is also the other.

l: identity of all things, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The identity of all things means that distinctions such as beam and pillar, ugliness and beauty, greatness and wickedness, construction and destruction, are brought together into one. The truly intelligent understand this by transferring themselves into the position of the things viewed.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: GOD is the refuge of the true Sage, who places himself in subjective relation with all things. The soul is described as an emanation from GOD, passing to and from the earth through the portals of Life and Death.

l: Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The true Sage rejects distinctions of this and that, regards contraries as identical, and adapts himself to the laws of Heaven. He keeps knowledge within himself, assigns without justifying by argument, and uses the light that comes out of darkness.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The universe and the speaker are said to have come into being together and to be one. Nothing in the universe is ultimately separable from the identity established through TAO.

l: Speech, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Speech is differentiated by meaning and becomes obscured by the gloss of the world. It cannot fully express TAO, and the unit questions whether speech itself belongs to either category of contraries.

l: mind, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The mind is subject to indecision, fear, concealment, passion, and other changing perturbations. It should be without fixed criteria, like a tabula rasa, so that it can accept things as they are rather than as they appear.

l: soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The soul is presented as the possible power that brings emotions and bodily functions into play, although its form cannot be seen. Its mandate ends with the exhaustion of the mortal body.

l: Confucian and Mihist schools, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The Confucian and Mihist schools obscure TAO through opposing affirmations and negations. Each denies what the other affirms and affirms what the other denies.

l: Hui Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: Hui Tzŭ is associated with the alternation theory of subjective and objective and with arguing about distinctions. His particular views differed from those of the world, and he ended in the obscurity of the hard and white.

l: the light of nature, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER II.
s: The light of nature enables affirmative and negative, and subjective and objective, to be reconciled. It is associated with having no established mental criteria and seeing all things as one.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The Emperor Yao considers attacking the Tsungs, Kueis, and Hsü-aos, but Shun argues that virtue should prevail through its influence rather than force. Yeh Ch'üeh and Wang I debate whether anything can be known, questioning standards of habitat, taste, beauty, and virtue. Chang Wu Tzŭ explains the Sage's unity beyond opposites, including right and wrong, life and death, and identifies dependence on Another as dependence upon God. The butterfly dream of Chuang Tzŭ illustrates uncertainty about whether he is a man dreaming of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming of being a man.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Shun says virtue should excel the suns and exert a superior influence, making active force unnecessary.

l: knowing and not knowing, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Wang I and Yeh Ch'üeh question whether knowing can be distinguished from not knowing. They conclude that human beings cannot be certain of their own judgments.

l: positive and negative, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Positive and negative are presented as opposites whose distinctions are obscured by human judgment. In the unity of God, their antagonism and distinctions are obliterated.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The Perfect Man is described as a spiritual being unaffected by heat, cold, thunder, storms, or what is bad for ordinary people. He passes beyond the external world, where death and life have no victory over him.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Death is presented as a state that may cause the dead to regret having clung to life. The Perfect Man passes beyond the power of death.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Love of life may be a delusion, and those who cling to life may later regret it. The text compares attachment to life with a dream from which awakening changes one's understanding.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Confucius is quoted as describing the true sage as unconcerned with mundane affairs and as adhering to TAO. Chang Wu Tzŭ says Confucius could not know the points on which the Yellow Emperor doubted and later includes Confucius among those who are dreams.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: TAO is associated with adhering without questioning, speaking without speaking, and roaming beyond the limits of the dusty world. Its embodiment is discussed through the Sage's harmonious unity.

l: Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The Sage blends everything into one harmonious whole, ignoring rank and precedence. The revolutions of ten thousand years and even the passing of the universe do not injure his Unity.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The Sage holds the universe in his grasp and blends its distinctions into harmony. The universe may pass away, but the Sage will still flourish.

l: dream, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Dreams can make people mistake lamentation, sorrow, banquets, and hunts for waking reality. The text suggests that ordinary life itself is a great dream and that people do not know they are dreaming until awakening.

l: Great Awakening, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The Great Awakening reveals that ordinary life is really a great dream. It is presented as a future realization of the nature of present experience.

l: right and wrong, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Human beings cannot determine with certainty whether an argument is right or wrong, even when one side defeats the other. The text advises passing beyond right and wrong into the Infinite.

l: Another, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Another is proposed as the one upon whom people must depend because no disputing person can decide the truth. Dependence on Another is said to be like no dependence at all.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: God is described as the Infinite whose unity embraces and obliterates distinctions. In God, contraries are merged without antagonism.

l: unity of God, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The unity of God is the all-embracing state in which positive and negative, right and wrong, this and that, are obliterated and merged. It provides refuge and perfect adaptation to whatever may happen.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: Chuang Tzŭ recounts dreaming that he was a butterfly and awakening as himself. He cannot determine whether he was a man dreaming of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming of being a man.

l: butterfly, Chuang Tzŭ, Of old, the Emperor Yao said to Shun, "I would smite the Tsungs, and
s: The butterfly appears in Chuang Tzŭ's dream as a being fluttering freely and unaware of human individuality. The dream leaves uncertain whether the butterfly or the man is the true dreamer.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: “Nourishment of the Soul” concerns the limits of life, the pursuit of knowledge, freedom, and the acceptance of death. Prince Hui’s cook explains how devotion to Tao and following natural openings preserve his chopper, teaching the Prince how to care for life. Lao Tzŭ’s death prompts Ch’in Shih to argue that birth and death occur according to eternal principles and should not provoke excessive grief. The unit concludes that a properly nourished soul may become immortal and return to the Great Unknown.

l: Nourishment of the Soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: “Nourishment of the Soul” concerns how to preserve life, fulfill one’s duties, and care for the soul through accommodation to circumstances, freedom, and acceptance of death.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Life has a limit, while knowledge is without limit, and pursuing the limitless through the limited is fatal. Life should be preserved by avoiding fame and disgrace, following a middle course, and respecting natural principles.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Death comes when it is a person’s time to die and is described as God cutting down a man suspended in the air. The ancients regarded excessive lamentation and sorrow at death as violations of eternal principles.

l: soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: The soul is what informs life and should be nourished rather than worn out with the body in mortal pursuits. If properly nourished, it may become immortal and return beatified to the Great Unknown.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Tao is greater than skill, and the cook has devoted himself to it. Following Tao means working with the mind, relying on eternal principles, and moving according to the natural constitution of things.

l: Prince Hui, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Prince Hui watches his cook cut up a bullock and praises his skill. From the cook’s explanation, Prince Hui learns how to take care of his life.

l: cook (Prince Hui's cook), Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Prince Hui’s cook says that he has devoted himself to Tao rather than merely cultivating skill. He follows natural openings and cavities, avoids cutting joints and large bones, and carefully handles hard parts, allowing him to use the same chopper for nineteen years.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Lao Tzŭ dies, causing people to mourn him intensely. Ch’in Shih argues that Lao Tzŭ’s words and tears had increased human emotion and forgotten the source from which life was received.

l: Ch'in Shih, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Ch’in Shih goes to mourn when Lao Tzŭ dies, utters three yells, and departs. He explains that excessive grief violates eternal principles because birth and death occur according to their proper times.

l: the Master (Lao Tzŭ), Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: The Master comes because it is his time to be born and goes because it is his time to die. His attachment to mourners is criticized as having encouraged words and tears that should not have been expressed.

l: the Infinite, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER III.
s: Immortality is presented as a possible state for the soul when it is duly nourished and not exhausted by the body’s mortal pursuits. The immortal soul may return beatified to the Great Unknown from which it came.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: Chapter IV, “Man among men,” concerns how people should conduct themselves among others through passivity, self-reformation, and resignation to TAO. Yen Hui seeks to reform the Prince of Wei, but Confucius teaches him that direct moral intervention will fail and instructs him in the fasting of the heart. Tzŭ Kao receives similar advice before a mission to the State of Ch'i: he should serve without attachment to success or failure and follow Destiny and Duty. Yen Ho is advised by Chü Poh Yü to adapt outwardly while preserving his inner standard when tutoring the eldest son of Prince Ling of the Wei State.

l: CHAPTER IV, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It presents teachings on how man should live among men, emphasizing passive virtue, self-reformation, and freedom from attachment to fame, success, and failure.

l: Man among men, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It concerns conduct among other people, especially adapting outwardly while preserving inner integrity and relying on TAO.

l: Yen Yüan, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He plans to visit the State of Wei to help its suffering people and reform the Prince of Wei. Confucius warns him against direct moral intervention and teaches him the fasting of the heart.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He advises Yen Hui, Tzŭ Kao, and Yen Ho to rely on TAO, restraint, inward cultivation, and acceptance of circumstances rather than forceful action.

l: Wei State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is described as suffering under poor government, with people dying and their corpses lying throughout the land.

l: Prince of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He is mature but unmanageable, disregards the State, fails to see his own faults, and takes pleasure in trampling on the feelings of others.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It should first be obtained for oneself and must not be distributed carelessly, since doing so causes uncertainty and mental disturbance. It guides successful action and can abide in a mind emptied of personal wisdom.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is said to result in a desire for fame, while its proper expression requires resignation, inward cultivation, and disregard for personal reward or punishment.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: They first obtained TAO for themselves before obtaining it for others. Their teachings can serve as a protective authority when a person speaks against wrongdoing.

l: fasting of the heart, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It consists not in abstaining from wine or flesh but in cultivating unity, allowing the mind to become empty and passively responsive to externals so that TAO can abide within it.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: A person who is inwardly straight is described as a servant of God and regards the Son of Heaven and himself as equally children of God.

l: Tzŭ Kao, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He is sent on an important mission to the State of Ch'i and fears both inner punishment from anxiety and outer punishment if he fails. Confucius tells him to serve without attachment to the act's outcome and to communicate in simple, restrained terms.

l: Ch'i State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is the destination of Tzŭ Kao's important mission, where he expects to receive respect but doubts that his hosts will share his interest in the matter.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is one of two sources of safety and governs circumstances such as a child's love for its parents. Confucius tells Tzŭ Kao to leave difficult outcomes to Destiny.

l: Duty, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is one of two sources of safety and includes a subject's allegiance to the sovereign. Its perfection lies in serving without attachment to the particular act.

l: Yen Ho, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He is about to tutor the eldest son of Prince Ling of the Wei State and asks Chü Poh Yü how to deal with a naturally low and dangerous disposition.

l: Prince Ling of the Wei State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He is the prince whose eldest son is to be tutored by Yen Ho.

l: Chü Poh Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He advises Yen Ho to reform himself, adapt outwardly without surrendering his inner standard, and avoid provoking the person he must influence.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: He is portrayed as manageable when properly managed but unmanageable when excited to fury. He is advised to rely on passive virtue and to avoid imposing superiority on others.

l: regeneration of all creation, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IV.
s: It is said to be possible through the passive method in which the senses communicate inwardly while the mind excludes its own wisdom.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: An artisan dismisses a sacred li tree as worthless timber, but the tree explains in a dream that its uselessness preserved it from harm and enabled it to reach old age. Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh sees a large tree on Shang mountain whose uselessness has allowed it to grow large. The unit contrasts useful trees and people, who are cut down, conscripted, or exploited, with useless or deformed ones who escape danger. Confucius encounters Chieh Yü, who warns that when TAO does not prevail, people should preserve themselves and that the use of useless things is not understood.

l: artisan, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: The artisan sees the sacred li tree but judges it worthless because its wood is unsuitable for boats, coffins, furniture, doors, and pillars. After dreaming that the tree spoke, he tells his apprentice about the dream.

l: apprentice (the artisan's apprentice), Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: The apprentice admires the sacred li tree and asks why the artisan ignored it. After hearing the dream, he asks how a tree that aimed at uselessness became sacred.

l: sacred li tree, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: The sacred li tree is large enough to shelter an ox and has many branches of boat-sized girth. It explains that its lack of usefulness protected it from being cut down and allowed it to live out its years, while becoming sacred helped it escape its enemies.

l: usefulness and uselessness, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Uselessness is presented as a means of preserving life from cutting, conscription, public works, and other dangers. The unit says that ordinary judgments cannot properly assess means adopted to reach the unusual goal of uselessness.

l: usefulness, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Useful trees are stripped, cut down, or felled because their fruit, timber, or other qualities are valued. The unit concludes that people understand the use of useful things but do not understand the use of useless things.

l: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Tzŭ Ch'i of Nan-poh sees a large tree on Shang mountain and recognizes that its uselessness has enabled it to attain great size. He suggests that a wise man might follow the tree's example to escape danger from his surroundings.

l: large tree (on Shang mountain), Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: The large tree shelters a thousand chariot teams, but its crooked branches, irregular grain, bitter leaves, and overpowering odor make it useless for ordinary purposes. Its uselessness is described as the reason it has grown so large.

l: hunchback Su, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Hunchback Su earns a living through tailoring, washing, and sifting rice, and his deformity protects him from conscription and public works. He receives grain and firewood, showing how physical deformity can preserve a person's life until its allotted end.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Confucius is in the Ch'u State when Chieh Yü passes his door and addresses him with a warning about virtue, political usefulness, and the need for caution.

l: Chieh Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Chieh Yü calls to Confucius that the phœnix's virtue has fallen and warns that people should preserve themselves when TAO does not prevail. He teaches that worldly honours are undervalued, misfortunes are hard to avoid, and useful things are harmed by their usefulness.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, A certain artisan was travelling to the Ch'i State. On reaching
s: Chieh Yü says that if TAO prevails on earth, prophets will fulfil their mission, but if TAO does not prevail, they will only preserve themselves. In the present age, he says, they will merely just escape.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Chapter V concerns the evidence of complete virtue, showing how inward virtue can produce outward influence while making outward form insignificant. Wang T'ai, Shên T'u Chia, No-toes, and Ai T'ai T'o are physically imperfect yet attract followers or command respect because of their inner virtue. Confucius teaches that the immortal soul endures beyond life and death, that all things are one, and that virtue arises from inner harmony with Destiny. The chapter concludes that the truly wise wear human forms without being ruled by human passions, following TAO and cultivating the divine.

l: Chapter V, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Chapter V presents the evidence of complete virtue through figures whose outward forms are imperfect but whose inward virtue influences others. It contrasts cultivation of the divine with dependence on human qualities, wisdom, skill, and outward appearance.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Virtue is shown as an inward harmony that can influence others without preaching, argument, power, or outward display. Complete virtue allows a person to accept changing conditions, live peacefully with mankind, and remain undisturbed by good and evil.

l: external self, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Outward form is treated as secondary to the inner principle that gives a body its value. The chapter teaches that virtue should prevail while outward form is forgotten.

l: Wang T'ai, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Wang T'ai has had his toes cut off, yet he has as many disciples as Confucius. He does not preach or discuss, but those who come to him empty depart full because he directs his mind toward the climax of virtue and sees all things as one.

l: Ch'ang Chi, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Ch'ang Chi asks Confucius how Wang T'ai can teach without preaching and how his mind functions despite his mutilation. He also challenges Confucius about Wang T'ai's self-directed cultivation and outward influence.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Confucius regards Wang T'ai as a prophet and says he would study under him. He teaches that the immortal soul is unaffected by life and death, that all things are one, and that inner stillness and harmony produce virtue.

l: Lu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: The State of Lu is the setting in which Wang T'ai and Shu Shan No-toes are presented. Wang T'ai's teaching is described as extending beyond the State of Lu to the whole world.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: TAO is identified with the doctrine that does not find expression in words. It gives man his expression, while God gives him his form, and it is associated with the condition in which distinctions do not disturb unity.

l: soul, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: The immortal soul is described as enduring when life and death pass away and when Heaven and Earth collapse. It can cause other things to change while preserving its own constitution intact.

l: Heaven, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Heaven is said to cover every man and, together with Earth, to support humanity. Confucius also describes the grace of Heaven as reaching Yao and Shun.

l: Earth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Earth supports every man and shows its grace through pines and cedars that remain green in winter and summer. It is invoked as a model of the universal conditions surrounding human life.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: God gives man his form and grants the divine nourishment by which the truly wise live. The grace of God is said to have reached Yao and Shun.

l: Life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Life and death are powerful but cannot affect the immortal soul. They are also among the changing conditions that revolve according to Destiny and should not disturb inner harmony.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Destiny governs changing conditions such as success and failure, poverty and wealth, and good and evil report. The virtuous person recognizes the inevitable, quietly acquiesces, and moves with the tide without offending others.

l: Shên T'u Chia, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Shên T'u Chia has had his toes cut off and studies under Poh Hun Wu Jen alongside Tzŭ Ch'an. He argues that accepting Destiny and focusing on the internal frees him from concern about his mutilation and from being dragged back to externals.

l: Tzŭ Ch'an, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Tzŭ Ch'an is a Minister of State from the Chêng State who studies with Shên T'u Chia. He initially insists on precedence because of his office, but Shên T'u Chia's rebuke causes him to fidget, change countenance, and ask him to stop.

l: No-toes, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: No-toes has been mutilated and walks on his heels to see Confucius, who first rebukes him for his misfortune. He leaves after Confucius's words, then asks Lao Tzŭ about Confucius's wisdom and says that Confucius's punishment by God makes him impossible to release.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Lao Tzŭ tells No-toes that Confucius could be freed from his fetters by being met with the continuity of life and death and the identity of can and cannot. No-toes replies that Confucius has been punished by God.

l: Duke Ai of the Lu State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Duke Ai asks Confucius about Ai T'ai T'o, a loathsome leper whom men and women nevertheless seek out. After hearing Confucius's explanation of perfect talents and virtue without outward form, Duke Ai becomes concerned that his own rule has harmed his State and regards Confucius as a moral friend.

l: Ai T'ai T'o, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Ai T'ai T'o is physically loathsome but inspires trust, sympathy, and attachment without preaching or exercising power. He accepts the offer to become Prime Minister of the Lu State, then soon leaves, demonstrating talents that are perfect and virtue without outward form.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Chuang Tzŭ argues that a man can have no passions in the sense of not allowing good and evil to disturb his internal economy. He says that TAO gives man expression and God gives him form, and criticizes Hui Tzŭ for devoting his intelligence to externals.

l: human passions, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Human passions are described as conditions that can disturb the internal economy and add to the sum of mortality. The truly wise wear human forms and associate with men but are not ruled by human passions.

l: good and evil, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER V.
s: Good and evil are among the opposites that should not disturb a person's internal economy. A person without passions falls in with whatever happens as a matter of course instead of allowing good and evil to disrupt inner harmony.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit concerns God, Man, TAO, and the relationship between the human and the divine. It describes the pure men of old as acting spontaneously, accepting life and death without passion, and harmonizing with all creation. It teaches that life, death, birth, and transitions belong to destiny, while TAO is the ultimate, formless principle underlying heaven, earth, the universe, and all existence. It presents human form and the countless transitions beyond it as sources of joy because the truly wise look toward what cannot be lost.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: God is described as a principle existing by its own intrinsicality and operating spontaneously without self-manifestation. Man emanates from God, and the divine finds expression in the human.

l: Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Man proceeds from God and should express on earth what God is for eternity in the universe. Man must recognize both the known and the unknown while working out his allotted span.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: TAO is the ultimate, formless principle with laws and evidences, devoid of action and form. It existed before heaven and earth, governs all transitions, and cannot be lost when the whole universe is concealed in the whole universe.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The pure men of old acted without calculation, plans, or attachment to success and failure. They accepted life and death without love or hatred, played their allotted parts cheerfully, and harmonized with all creation.

l: human and divine relationship, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The human and the divine are related because Man emanates from God, but knowledge depends on fulfilment and the distinction between the two cannot be fully known before death. Pure men allow no conflict between the human and the divine because both what they care for and what they do not care for are reduced to ONE.

l: Wisdom, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Knowledge requires fulfilment, which is uncertain during life. A person knows God by recognizing his own divine origin and knows Man by resting in the known while waiting for knowledge of the unknown.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Life is an allotted span in which a person should complete his course without perishing in mid-career. TAO gives life its form, toil in manhood, repose in old age, and rest in death.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Death lifts the veil and reveals that life is bounded at each end by immortality to which the soul finally reverts. The pure men of old neither loved life nor hated death and accepted dissolution as part of their allotted course.

l: the Infinite, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Immortality bounds life at each end, though this is not truly known until death. The soul finally reverts to an immortality associated with TAO.

l: Destiny, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Life and death belong to destiny, whose sequence is as inevitable as day and night and beyond human interference. Destiny includes early death, old age, a beginning, and an end.

l: Heaven, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Heaven is part of the reality that did not yet exist when TAO already existed. The Yellow Emperor obtained TAO and soared upon the clouds to heaven, while Fu Yüeh was enrolled among the stars of heaven.

l: Earth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Earth, like heaven, came after TAO, which existed before both. The universe became visible through TAO, and earth is included in the whole creation governed by it.

l: THE UNIVERSE, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The universe is described as something that can be concealed in the whole universe, leaving no place where it may be lost. It became what can be seen through TAO, which underlies all its phenomena.

l: birth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The pure men of old did not rejoice in birth or strive to postpone dissolution. Birth is treated as one of the conditions included within the transitions governed by destiny.

l: transitions, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: The wise accept countless transitions with only the infinite to look forward to. These transitions are viewed as incomparable bliss because TAO endures through them.

l: human life span, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: A person should work out his allotted span and not perish in mid-career. The span includes toil in manhood, repose in old age, and the eventual rest of death.

l: death transition, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VI.
s: Death is presented as a transition through which the soul returns to immortality and toward TAO. Accepting death as naturally as early death, old age, a beginning, and an end is described as a step toward wisdom.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei asks Nü Yü how he remains youthful, and Nü Yü explains that TAO was transmitted through progressive detachment from distinctions, the external world, and personal existence. Four friends accept Inaction, Life, and Death as the conditions of friendship, and their illnesses and deaths are treated as transformations governed by God, Nature, and TAO. Confucius explains to Tzŭ Kung that certain men live beyond conventional rules, identifying TAO as what sustains human beings. The unit also presents Mêng Sun Ts'ai's natural mourning, Yen Hui's gradual abandonment of charity, duty, ceremony, music, body, and mind, and Tzŭ Sang's reflection that poverty comes from Destiny.

l: Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei asks Nü Yü how his countenance remains like that of a child despite his age. He also asks how Nü Yü obtained TAO.

l: Nü Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Nü Yü says that he has learnt TAO and describes teaching it to Pu Liang I. He explains that Pu Liang I passed beyond worldly distinctions, the external world, and awareness of his own existence, ultimately becoming able to enter where life and death are no more.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: TAO is presented as something learned through books, learning, investigation, co-ordination, application, desire to know, the unknown, the great void, and infinity. It makes life and death one, allows natural adaptation to circumstances, and is what human beings need in order to live in peace.

l: Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: A sage is described as having qualifications that do not necessarily include TAO. A perfect sage can pass beyond worldly distinctions, the external world, and personal existence.

l: life, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Life is described as the backbone of existence and as a state granted when its time has come. TAO gives life its form, toil in manhood, repose in old age, and rest in death.

l: death, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Death is described as the tail of existence and as a transformation governed by the same law that grants life. In TAO, death and life are one, and death releases the living from a huge tumour.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: God is described as governing transformation and as the caster who shapes beings in the universe's smelting-pot. Human beings are said to return to God, and man is said to have always yielded before God.

l: Inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Inaction is made the head of existence in the resolution accepted by four friends. It is also associated with the state in which men wander beyond mortality and conventionality.

l: four friends, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: The four friends agree that whoever makes Inaction the head, Life the backbone, and Death the tail of existence may join their friendship. They look at each other, smile, and become friends without further discussion.

l: Tzŭ Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Tzŭ Yü becomes severely physically deformed through illness, but says that his mental equilibrium remains undisturbed. He accepts death as a natural transformation and is not afraid of it.

l: Tzŭ Lai, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Tzŭ Lai becomes gravely ill and accepts that Nature may send him wherever it chooses. He compares the universe to a smelting-pot and himself to metal that will be shaped by God.

l: Nature, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Nature is identified with a man's parents and is said to command him as parents command a son. It gives human beings their forms, labor, old age, and death.

l: Tzŭ Sang Hu, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Tzŭ Sang Hu converses with Mêng Tzŭ Fan and Tzŭ Ch'in Chang about being and not being, doing and not doing, and wandering beyond the limits of space. After his death, one of his companions sings beside his corpse, and Confucius explains that such men travel beyond the rule of life.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Confucius sends Tzŭ Kung to mourn Tzŭ Sang Hu, then explains that Tzŭ Sang Hu's companions live beyond conventional rules and distinctions. He teaches that man is born in TAO and that human beings can live in peace by obtaining TAO.

l: Tzŭ Kung, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Tzŭ Kung questions the singing of Tzŭ Sang Hu's companion beside the corpse and asks Confucius what kind of men they are. He also asks why people should follow conventional rules and asks about divine men.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Human beings are described as being born in TAO and as needing TAO in order to live peacefully. They are also portrayed as subject to dreams, mortality, social conventions, and transformations of life and death.

l: Sages of old, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Divine men are described as divine in relation to human beings but ordinary in relation to God. The meanest being in heaven is said to be better than the best being on earth.

l: Mêng Sun Ts'ai, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Mêng Sun Ts'ai mourns his mother's death without snivelling, heartfelt grief, or howling, yet he is considered the best mourner in the State of Lu. Confucius explains that he follows outward requirements while remaining inwardly free from disturbance and accepts life and death as natural transitions.

l: Yen Yüan, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: Yen Hui successively says that he has discarded charity and duty, ceremonial and music, and finally everything. He describes freeing himself from body and reasoning powers and becoming one with the Infinite.

l: the Infinite, Chuang Tzŭ, Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei
s: The Infinite is what Yen Hui becomes one with after discarding body and mind. Confucius says that attaining this state removes bias and makes one without beginning or end.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: This unit concerns how to govern through inaction, natural laws, and TAO rather than coercive laws and personal effort. Yeh Ch'üeh, Chien Wu, T'ien Kên, Yang Tzŭ Chü, and others learn that the truly wise ruler governs invisibly by perfecting himself and following natural order. Hu Tzŭ demonstrates different manifestations of TAO to Chi Han, leading Lieh Tzŭ to abandon artificiality and practice passivity. Shu and Hu kill Hun Tun by boring holes in him, illustrating the perils of action.

l: How to Govern, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It teaches that princes should reign rather than rule, and that government should follow natural laws through inaction rather than impose artificial laws.

l: Yeh Ch'üeh, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He asks Wang I four questions that Wang I cannot answer, and becomes delighted because he takes this as discovering that ignorance is true knowledge.

l: Wang I, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He cannot answer Yeh Ch'üeh's four questions.

l: artificial, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It arises when rulers rely on self-created standards, charity, laws, regulations, and deliberate efforts instead of natural order.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It is presented as the basis of invisible government, natural action without self, and the state beyond artificiality. Hu Tzŭ shows its manifestations to Chi Han, while Lieh Tzŭ learns that he has not yet acquired real knowledge of it.

l: Chien Wu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is taught laws and regulations developed by princes, but Chieh Yü tells him that this teaching is false.

l: Chieh Yü, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He rejects governing mankind through imposed laws and says the truly wise man governs without concern for externals.

l: laws and regulations, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: They are described as standards evolved by princes that people are expected to hear and obey, but attempting to govern mankind through them is condemned.

l: princes, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: They are said to create artificial laws and should reign rather than rule.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It should not be governed through coercive laws and regulations, but allowed to follow natural order.

l: the truly wise man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He first perfects himself and then accomplishes what he wants without external force. His government follows natural order and has no concern with externals.

l: T'ien Kên, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He asks a Sage about governing the empire and is told to resolve mental energy into abstraction, physical energy into inaction, and follow natural order without self.

l: Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He initially rejects T'ien Kên's question about government, then explains that the empire will be governed when people follow natural order without self.

l: Yang Tzŭ Chü, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He asks Lao Tzŭ whether an ardent, courageous, knowledgeable, and tireless pursuer of TAO would be a wise ruler, and asks what wise government consists in.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He says that energetic cleverness and deliberate pursuit make a ruler a mere handicraftsman. He teaches that a wise ruler's goodness influences the whole empire invisibly and is based upon the baseless.

l: the Sage, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: His goodness covers the whole empire and influences all creation, while he himself seems unaware of it and leaves no conscious trace.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It is best governed through natural laws, inaction, and invisible influence rather than coercion or imposed artificiality.

l: Chi Han, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is a magician who predicts events with supernatural accuracy. After seeing Hu Tzŭ in several manifestations, he becomes confused and flees.

l: Lieh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is initially infatuated with Chi Han's powers and thinks he knows something more perfect than Hu Tzŭ's TAO. After Hu Tzŭ's demonstrations, he becomes convinced that he lacks real knowledge, practices in earnest for three years, and reverts to the natural.

l: Hu Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He demonstrates successive manifestations of TAO to Chi Han, appearing as earth, heaven, harmonious equilibrium, and a great blank. His demonstrations cause Lieh Tzŭ to recognize his ignorance.

l: Inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It brings fame, makes one a centre of thought and responsibility, and allows compliance with divine principles without outward display. It is identified with passivity.

l: Perfect Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He employs his mind as a mirror: he grasps nothing, refuses nothing, receives without keeping, and triumphs over matter without injuring himself.

l: Shu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is the ruler of the southern sea and, with Hu, decides to repay Hun Tun's kindness by boring holes in him.

l: Hu, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is the ruler of the northern sea and joins Shu in boring seven holes in Hun Tun.

l: Hun Tun, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: He is the ruler of the central zone and has no holes for seeing, hearing, eating, or breathing. Shu and Hu bore one hole each day, and he dies on the seventh day.

l: death of Hun Tun, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It results from Shu and Hu's attempt to improve Hun Tun by boring seven holes in him, illustrating the perils of action.

l: action, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It is portrayed as dangerous when imposed on what should follow natural order; Shu and Hu's action causes Hun Tun's death.

l: natural laws, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: They lead to the desired end without human interference and should guide the government of the empire.

l: government, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VII.
s: It is achieved when mental and physical energy are resolved into abstraction and inaction, and when people follow natural order without admitting the element of self.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The chapter argues that joined toes and extra fingers are natural but functionally superfluous additions, and uses them to criticize artificial charity and duty to one's neighbour. It presents TAO as natural perfection that should not be imposed through ceremonies, music, argument, or moral instruction. The chapter concerns Confucianism and claims that pursuing reputation, wealth, fame, or moral ideals can injure human nature. It concludes that true perfection lies in cultivating TAO and understanding oneself rather than imitating others.

l: joined toes, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Joined toes are described as natural but functionally superfluous lumps of flesh. Dividing them causes pain, illustrating the sorrow caused by trying to alter natural conditions.

l: extra fingers, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Extra fingers are described as natural but functionally superfluous excrescences. Biting one off causes pain, illustrating that both excess and deficiency can produce the same sorrow.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: TAO is presented as the natural perfection of things, requiring no artificial additions or external imposition. Its cultivation involves yielding to natural conditions and seeing oneself rather than others.

l: charity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Charity is portrayed as an artificial addition when intentionally cultivated for reputation or applause. The chapter argues that preaching charity changes human nature and is not part of the natural moral constitution.

l: duty to one's neighbour, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Duty to one's neighbour is treated like intentional charity: an artificial virtue imposed on natural life. The chapter claims that pursuing it has caused sorrow, changed human nature, and distracted people from TAO.

l: Confucianism, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Confucianism is the target of the chapter's violent tirade. Its leading doctrines, especially charity, duty to one's neighbour, ceremonies, music, and moral reputation, are criticized as harmful artificial additions to natural life.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: This unit concerns horses, Poh Loh, the people, Sages, and the government of the empire. It contrasts horses’ natural lives with the harmful effects of branding, bridling, shackling, and other artificial management imposed by Poh Loh. It argues that government makes the same mistake when it suppresses natural instincts through charity, duty to one’s neighbour, music, and ceremonies. The text presents natural integrity and Tao as preferable to the systems introduced by artisans and Sages.

l: horses, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Horses naturally live on dry land, eat grass, drink water, and express pleasure or anger through simple physical actions. Poh Loh’s branding, clipping, hoof-paring, halters, shackles, stables, training, grooming, and whipping kill many horses and deprave their natural dispositions.

l: Poh Loh, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Poh Loh claims to understand the management of horses. He brands, clips, pares, restrains, stables, trains, grooms, trims, and whips horses, causing many of them to die and their natures to become depraved.

l: government, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: The government of the empire is said to make the same mistake as Poh Loh by imposing artificial systems on natural human life. It is discussed as harmful when it departs from natural instincts and Tao.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: The empire was divided against itself when Sages introduced music, ceremonies, charity, and duty to one’s neighbour. Its people later developed a taste for knowledge and competed for gain under the influence of these teachings.

l: Man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: The people have natural instincts to weave and clothe themselves and to till and feed themselves. In the days when natural instincts prevailed, they lived quietly, moved freely, and were naturally integrated; under the Sages, they became interested in knowledge and struggled for gain.

l: Sages, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Sages are blamed for tripping people up with charity and fettering them with duty to one’s neighbour. They introduced music and ceremonies to rectify government and caused people to develop a taste for knowledge and competition for gain.

l: Ho Hsü, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Ho Hsü is identified as a legendary ruler of old. In his days, people did little when at rest, went nowhere particular when moving, rejoiced when they had food, and strolled about with full bellies.

l: natural instincts, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Natural instincts include weaving and clothing oneself and tilling and feeding oneself, and they are described as common to all humanity and Heaven-sent. When they prevailed, people lived quietly and retained natural integrity.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Tao is presented as something that was abandoned in order to practise charity and duty to one’s neighbour. The text implies that preserving Tao would leave no need for those artificial practices.

l: natural integrity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Natural integrity is described as the condition in which people, equally without knowledge and evil desires, remain in a state of natural perfection. Its destruction permits the production of artificial articles and systems.

l: duty to one's neighbour, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Charity and duty to one’s neighbour are introduced by Sages as teachings used to shape government and satisfy people’s hearts. Their introduction disturbs natural life and contributes to division, knowledge-seeking, and competition for gain.

l: music and ceremonies, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER IX.
s: Music and ceremonies are introduced by Sages to rectify the form of government and are associated with the division of the empire. The text questions their necessity when natural instincts and Tao remain intact.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: The unit argues that artificial restrictions, measures, laws, and wisdom protect strong thieves rather than preventing theft. It concerns T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ's seizure of the State of Ch'i, Robber Chê's use of the Sages' principles, and the harmful effects of charity, duty, knowledge, and disputation. It concludes that abolishing imposed wisdom and restrictions would allow people to return to natural integrity and Tao.

l: Opening Trunks, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Opening trunks represents the use of cords, bolts, and locks as artificial precautions against thieves. The unit argues that such precautions assist strong thieves who can carry away the entire trunk or till.

l: restrictions, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Restrictions are described as artificial fetters that protect strong thieves and cause people to depart from their natural state. The unit calls for their utter abolition so that people may become fit for the reception of Tao.

l: thieves, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Thieves are deterred by cords, bolts, locks, measures, scales, tallies, signets, and punishments, but these devices are also stolen or used to increase their profits. Petty thieves are associated with jade, pearls, tallies, signets, measures, and scales, while great thieves steal States and their principles.

l: strong thief, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: The strong thief carries off the till with box and bag and fears only that the cords and locks may not be strong enough. The unit says that the world's wit and wisdom serve as assistance and protection to such thieves.

l: Ch'i State, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: The State of Ch'i was prosperous and governed according to rules laid down by the Sages. T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew its Prince, stole the kingdom and the Sages' wisdom-tricks, and his descendants ruled Ch'i for twelve generations.

l: Sages, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: The Sages' wisdom and restrictions are said to cause the appearance and protection of great robbers. The unit calls for the Sages and their imposed systems to disappear so that the people may return to natural integrity and the empire may rest in peace.

l: T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i and stole the State of Ch'i along with the wisdom-tricks obtained from the Sages. Although he acquired the reputation of a thief, he lived as comfortably as Yao or Shun, and his descendants ruled Ch'i for twelve generations.

l: Robber Chê, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Robber Chê teaches that thieving contains wisdom, courage, heroism, shrewdness, and justice in dividing spoil. The unit says that the doctrine of the Sages is indispensable to him and that doubling the Sages' wisdom would double his profits.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Tao is presented as the natural condition for which people become fit when the restrictions of the Sages are abolished. Rulers who pursue knowledge while neglecting Tao bring confusion upon the empire.

l: charity, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Charity and duty to one's neighbour are described as integral parts of princedom that a ruler can steal together with a State and the Sages' wisdom. The unit calls for them to be discarded so that the people's virtue may become one with God.

l: wisdom and knowledge, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER X.
s: Wisdom and knowledge are portrayed as instruments that protect great thieves, create artificial distinctions, and bring confusion to the world. The unit says that love of knowledge lies at the bottom of great confusion because people pursue what they do not know and dispute what they do not excel in.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The unit contrasts letting alone with government, arguing that coercion and over-refinement disturb mankind’s natural conditions and virtue. It presents Inaction and TAO as the means by which rulers can support the empire without interfering with the natural goodness of the human heart. The Yellow Emperor learns from Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ that self-preservation, stillness, and harmony with heaven and earth lead toward perfect TAO. The Spirit of the Clouds learns from the Vital Principle that government causes disorder and that feeding the people with one’s heart and resting in inaction allows the world to flourish. The unit concludes by distinguishing the TAO of God from the TAO of man and describing how the perfect man and Sage act without premeditated interference.

l: letting alone, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Letting alone protects mankind from having natural dispositions perverted and virtue laid aside. It is presented as something that has existed with success, unlike governing mankind.

l: government, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Government is blamed for disturbing natural conditions, corrupting virtue, and producing disorder through rewards, punishments, coercion, and interference. The unit teaches that government should rest in inaction and avoid managing people as if they were mere things.

l: Inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Inaction allows people and the world to adapt to natural conditions and brings things to maturity without premeditated interference. A ruler who practices it can support and govern the State while avoiding harm to internal economy and natural goodness.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: TAO is described as profoundly mysterious, eternal, infinite, and connected with the original constitution of all things. Its way is expressed through inaction and compliance, while action and entanglement belong to the TAO of man.

l: man, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Mankind loses steadiness when excessive joy and sorrow displace its centre of gravity. Mankind is also harmed when rulers try to manage people as if they were mere things.

l: natural conditions of existence, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Natural conditions of existence require no artificial aids and should guide human life and government. Adapting to them prevents the eight forms of refinement from becoming hindrances and spoilers.

l: Virtue, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Virtue is weakened by dissatisfaction, discontent, and interference with natural dispositions. Without virtue, the empire cannot have stability.

l: the Empire, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The empire becomes unstable when rulers pursue rewards, punishments, knowledge, coercion, and excessive refinement. It can flourish when those in power rest in inaction and allow things to return to their original constitution.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Lao Tzŭ teaches that the natural goodness of the human heart should not be interfered with. He also states that governing the empire should be approached through inaction.

l: human heart, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The human heart can be forced down or stirred up, and either treatment has a fatal issue. It may be softened by gentleness, but cutting and polishing it makes it unstable and uncontrollable.

l: Yellow Emperor, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Yellow Emperor initially seeks to govern heaven and earth, control the Two Powers, secure harvests, and feed his people. After Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ rebukes his interference, he resigns the Throne, withdraws into solitude, and learns about preserving the self through perfect TAO.

l: Confucianists, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Confucianists arise after the empire has already become troubled by interference with natural goodness. They preach amid cangues and fetters, although the unit presents their teachings as contributing to the conditions that produced those restraints.

l: Mihists, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Mihists arise alongside the Confucianists during a period of rivalry, fraud, recrimination, slander, and decadence. They also preach amid cangues and fetters after coercion has brought confusion into the empire.

l: Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ tells the Yellow Emperor that governing has disturbed heaven and earth and prevented perfect TAO. He teaches that stillness, purity, withdrawal from external knowledge, and preservation of the self lead to enduring life and harmony.

l: Spirit of the Clouds, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Spirit of the Clouds worries that heaven and earth are out of harmony and seeks advice on nourishing living beings. The Vital Principle tells him that government is the source of the disorder and teaches him to feed the people with his heart, rest in inaction, and release intelligence.

l: Vital Principle, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Vital Principle wanders without knowing what he wants or where he is going, simply awaiting events. He identifies government as the poison causing disorder and advises the Spirit of the Clouds to return to natural conditions and let all things flourish without knowledge.

l: heaven and earth, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: Heaven and earth fall out of harmony when government interferes, causing irregular seasons, disturbed influences, and disorder among living things. Their proper relationship is restored through inaction and compliance with natural conditions.

l: God, Chuang Tzŭ, CHAPTER XI.
s: God is associated with the TAO of God, whose way consists in inaction and compliance. The true Sage looks up to God but does not offer to aid.
